claims.text: The starting catalyst is a multi-element automotive alloy containing platinum-group and base metals in nearly equiatomic ratios.
Mild acid etching followed by controlled thermal annealing induces noble-metal surface segregation.
The acid-etching and annealing treatment forms a Pt-rich shell around a high-entropy-alloy core.
The resulting noble-metal-enriched shell is thin and stabilized.
The thermal-chemical treatment preferentially migrates the more noble components to the surface.
A Pt-rich shell enhances corrosion resistance.
The noble-metal-enriched shell resists attack by H2O and NO.
The shell minimizes degradation during thermal aging.
The shell preserves catalytically active sites during exhaust operation.
The core-shell architecture can enhance catalytic performance while maintaining low platinum-group-metal use.
Relative to the untreated catalyst, the treated catalyst will retain significantly more activity and durability under transient, low-temperature exhaust conditions.
The treatment will reduce deactivation over time.
The untreated alloy loses catalytic activity and durability under transient low-temperature operation, H2O/NO exposure, and thermal aging.
Overly aggressive etching or annealing may remove active sites or disrupt the alloy's beneficial structure.
Operating conditions more extreme than the simulated range may still cause degradation.
A treated-versus-untreated comparison under identical H2O/NO exposure and thermal cycling can test the hypothesis.
Failure to achieve a statistically significant improvement, operationalized as less than a 15–20% difference in degradation rate, would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The treatment is called a 'one-step' or single intervention, but it explicitly contains two sequential operations: acid etching and subsequent thermal annealing.
